content: Snakebite envenoming is a neglected tropical disease (NTD) that causes significant suffering, disability, and premature death across all continents. It is estimated that there are 7 million cases of envenoming and between 81,000 and 138,000 deaths annually. The economic burden of snakebite envenoming is overwhelming in many countries, particularly in lowand middle-income regions where social security systems are often absent. This burden extends beyond the victims themselves, frequently affecting entire families, especially in impoverished communities. The World Health Organization (WHO) has recognized the urgent need to address this issue. Following recommendations from its Strategic and Technical Advisory Group for Neglected Tropical Diseases and a resolution adopted by the Seventy-first World Health Assembly in 2018, snakebite envenoming has been added to the list of Category A NTDs. WHO has developed a comprehensive strategy aimed at reducing mortality and disability from snakebite envenoming by 50% by the year 2030. The strategy emphasizes the importance of community education to raise awareness about the risks of snakebites and to encourage individuals to seek timely medical care. It also focuses on improving case management, including first aid, effective and affordable treatment by well-trained medical staff, and rehabilitation services to help victims recover and return to productive lives. A critical component of the strategy is ensuring access to safe, effective, and affordable antivenoms. This involves building a stable and sustainable market for antivenoms, ensuring their production meets internationally accepted quality standards, and addressing the current crisis in antivenom supply. WHO plans to establish a revolving stockpile of proven, effective antivenoms to ensure their availability in regions where they are most needed. The strategy also aims to strengthen health systems by integrating snakebite prevention, treatment, and management into national health plans and policy frameworks. This will be achieved using the principles of the WHO Health Systems Framework. Additionally, partnerships, coordination, and resource mobilization will be essential to implement this comprehensive plan of action. Advocacy efforts will focus on building a global coalition to drive change, generate investment, and accelerate research into new therapies, diagnostics, and medical interventions. The strategy will be tested in 10–12 high-burden countries during 2019–2020, with support provided to design and implement locally relevant plans. During the scaling-up phase from 2021 to 2024, an additional 35–40 countries will be involved as resources increase and the effectiveness of the strategy is demonstrated. By the full roll-out phase from 2025 to 2030, all countries will have the opportunity to integrate the strategy into their public health agendas. WHO will regularly review and adapt the strategy to ensure it meets the needs of countries. Through sustained advocacy, WHO aims to build a global coalition committed to achieving the targets and milestones necessary to halve the number of snakebite deaths and cases of disability by 2030.
